title: Computational Complexity: P, NP & Reductions
summary: Complexity classes, polynomial-time reductions, and how to argue NP-completeness — the single most interview-relevant theory-of-computation topic.

slides.markdown:
Complexity theory classifies **decision problems** (yes/no questions) by how much time an algorithm needs to solve them, as input size grows. The headline question: **P vs NP**.

![P, NP, and NP-complete as nested/overlapping classes](assets/p-np-venn.svg)

`P` = solvable fast. `NP` = a proposed answer can be *checked* fast. Whether every NP problem is secretly also in P is the most famous open question in computer science.

assets.alt: P, NP, and NP-complete as nested/overlapping classes

slides.subTitle: P
slides.markdown:
**P** is the class of decision problems solvable in **polynomial time** — `O(n^k)` for some constant `k` — as input size `n` grows. This is the informal definition of "efficiently solvable."

Examples: sorting, shortest path (Dijkstra), checking if a number is prime, matching in bipartite graphs. All have known algorithms whose runtime grows as a polynomial in input size, not exponentially.

`P` is the class of problems you'd actually expect to run in production at real scale without special-casing.

slides.subTitle: NP
slides.markdown:
**NP** = problems where a *proposed solution* can be **verified** in polynomial time, even if finding that solution might take much longer.

Common misconception: **NP does not stand for "not polynomial."** It stands for **nondeterministic polynomial time** — and every problem in `P` is also in `NP` (if you can solve it fast, you can trivially verify a solution fast too).

Sudoku is the classic example: solving a hard Sudoku might take a while, but checking a completed grid is fast — that gap between "solve" and "verify" difficulty is exactly what defines NP.

slides.subTitle: NP-complete vs NP-hard
slides.markdown:
These two terms get conflated constantly.

| | NP-complete | NP-hard |
|---|---|---|
| Must be in NP (verifiable fast)? | Yes | Not necessarily |
| Relation to every NP problem | Every NP problem reduces to it | Every NP problem reduces to it |
| Example | 3-SAT, vertex cover | The halting problem (NP-hard, but not in NP — not even decidable) |

Every NP-complete problem is NP-hard, but not every NP-hard problem is in NP — NP-hard just means "at least as hard as the hardest NP problems," with no upper bound implied.

slides.subTitle: Polynomial-time reductions
slides.markdown:
A **polynomial-time reduction** from problem `A` to problem `B` is an efficient transformation: convert any instance of `A` into an instance of `B`, such that solving `B` immediately solves `A`.

If `A` reduces to `B` and `A` is known hard, `B` is at least as hard — a fast algorithm for `B` would give you a fast algorithm for `A` too, contradiction.

This is the entire machinery behind proving new problems NP-hard: find a known-hard problem, and show it reduces (efficiently) into your new problem.

slides.subTitle: Cook-Levin: SAT is NP-complete
slides.markdown:
The **Cook-Levin theorem** (1971) proved that **Boolean satisfiability (SAT)** — is there a true/false assignment making a Boolean formula true — is NP-complete, by simulating any NP-verifying Turing machine's computation as a giant Boolean formula. It was the *first* problem proven NP-complete.

This unlocked the field: once one problem is NP-complete, every later proof can just reduce from SAT instead of repeating that hard construction from scratch — SAT is the historical anchor everything else builds on.

A short list worth recognizing on sight:

- **3-SAT** — SAT restricted to clauses of exactly 3 literals (still NP-complete).
- **Vertex cover** — smallest set of vertices touching every edge.
- **Traveling salesman (decision version)** — is there a tour under length `k`?
- **Knapsack (decision version)** — can you hit value `≥ V` within weight `≤ W`?
- **Clique** — does a graph contain a fully-connected subgraph of size `k`?

Recognizing that a new problem "smells like" one of these is often the fastest path to guessing (and then proving) it's NP-hard.

slides.subTitle: The reduction recipe
slides.markdown:
The standard interview recipe for proving `X` is NP-hard:

1. **Pick** a known NP-complete problem that looks structurally similar (vertex cover, 3-SAT, clique).
2. **Construct** a polynomial-time transformation from an instance of that problem into `X`.
3. **Prove** the transformation is correct both ways: yes maps to yes, no maps to no.
4. **Conclude**: the known problem reduces to `X`, so `X` is NP-hard too.

The hard part is almost always step 2 — finding the right encoding.

slides.subTitle: P vs NP
slides.markdown:
Nobody has proven whether `P = NP` — it's one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, worth $1M unsolved. Most believe `P ≠ NP` (verifying is genuinely easier than solving, for some problems), but no proof exists either way.

Why it matters: a constructive proof of `P = NP` would mean every "needs exponential search" problem (cryptography, optimization, scheduling) has a hidden polynomial algorithm — breaking most public-key cryptography overnight.

Until resolved, "NP-hard" is treated as a practical certificate of hardness, even though it's technically unproven that no fast algorithm exists.

slides.subTitle: Practical strategies
slides.markdown:
Proving a problem NP-hard isn't the end of the conversation — it's the start of choosing a practical strategy:

- **Approximation algorithms** — guarantee a solution within some provable factor of optimal (e.g. a 2-approximation for vertex cover).
- **Heuristics** — greedy (Area 1 `greedy`) or local search, no guarantee but fast and often good enough in practice.
- **Exact but exponential** — dynamic programming (Area 1 `dynamic-programming`), exponential worst-case but fast on real inputs (small knapsack capacities).

slides.subTitle: Restricting the input
slides.markdown:
One more lever: **restrict the input**. Many NP-hard problems become polynomial on special structures — vertex cover is polynomial on trees, independent set is polynomial on bounded-degree graphs.

The interview signal to send: NP-hard doesn't mean "give up" — it means "pick the right trade-off (approximation, heuristic, exact-but-slow, or restricted input) deliberately, and say why."
